name: Chromium zlib (third_party/zlib fork)
workload: Inflate of gzip and zlib-wrapped streams (snappy corpus), raw CRC-32, and PNG decoding with SSE4.2/PCLMUL crc32, adler32 SIMD and chunk-copy inflate.
claimed_speedup: CRC-32 5x-25x faster than zlib's default BYFOUR crc32; gzip and zlib-wrapped inflate 69% and 50% faster on the snappy corpus; PNG decoding 4% faster from crc32 alone and 40% total combined with adler32 SIMD and inflate chunk copy.
compiler_and_flags: -msse4.2 -mpclmul for the SIMD crc32 translation unit; benchmark flags not stated
stars_or_usage: Ships in Chrome; github.com/chromium/chromium mirror 24.9k stars
tradeoffs: Tied to Chromium's build (BUILD.gn, runtime CPU detection, symbol renaming via names.h); x86, Arm and RISC-V SIMD paths; heavily patched inflate (inffast_chunk) means it does not track upstream zlib cleanly.
caveats: Numbers come from a first-party commit message (the SSE4.2 crc32 change) with no CPU model, compiler or benchmark code stated; older figures. Newer inflate and 64-bit SWAR work in later commits has no numbers I could open. madler/zlib issue 346 mentions the fork's optimizations but gives no data. Overlaps in goal with the already-listed cloudflare/zlib, matbech/zlib and zlib-ng. Repo is the whole Chromium mirror; the code is in third_party/zlib.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Chromium zlib optimizations SIMD inflate crc32 faster than zlib blog'; commit opened via the github.com mirror (chromium.googlesource.com is egress-blocked).

name: fdeflate
baseline: zlib-rs and zlib-ng (zlib-compatible deflate/inflate); also compared with miniz_oxide and libdeflate on the plot
workload: Deflate compression levels 1-7 and decompression of PNG-style data, measured with corpus-bench on the QOI benchmark corpus.
claimed_speedup: Compression: 'meaningfully outperforms zlib-rs for levels 1-3 and is slightly better for levels 4-7'; ultra-fast mode 'several times faster than other modes'; decoder 'rivals or exceeds' zlib-ng and zlib-rs.
stars_or_usage: 38 stars; compression backend of the png crate
tradeoffs: Rust crate with no C API shown; safe Rust without unsafe. Optimised for PNG-style data (many literals), levels 8-9 not implemented, compressor still under development (0.4.x), ultra-fast mode uses one block, one fixed Huffman tree and no distance codes except zero runs, so ratio is low.
caveats: Results are a plot image in a discussion post that I could not read as text (numbers not extracted); the README calls them preliminary. Baseline is zlib-rs/zlib-ng, not upstream zlib directly. No CPU or compiler stated. The qualitative claims were verified in the README. Not callable from C++ without writing a binding.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'zune-inflate OR fdeflate faster than zlib libdeflate PNG inflate benchmark'

name: Intel QPL (IAA hardware deflate path)
workload: RocksDB compression/decompression with Intel IAA offload on 4th-gen Xeon (per Intel tuning guide), plus DuckDB and HTSlib tests in third-party papers.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: throughput 92%-205% higher and p99 read latency 53%-74% lower than zlib-ng, with 5%-9% larger output; 34%-95% higher throughput and 23%-51% lower p99 read latency than zstd. Third-party snippets: DuckDB Deflate IAA 4.59 GB/s compress and 18.24 GB/s decompress, about 1.8x and 5.5x versus CPU execution.
hardware: Intel Sapphire Rapids Xeon (4th gen) with IAA accelerator
tradeoffs: Needs IAA hardware on Sapphire Rapids or later for the fast path; software fallback is the only option elsewhere. Deflate format only, ratio is lower than zstd. Related shim intel/zlib-accel (Apache-2.0) offloads whole-stream zlib calls to QAT/IAA or igzip but ships no benchmarks and has no streaming support on the accelerators.
caveats: Snippet only: the Intel guide (Tuning Guide for RocksDB Compression and Decompression with Intel IAA), the CMU/VLDB ADMS 2025 paper and the HTSlib paper were EGRESS_BLOCKED, so no page with the numbers was opened and benchmark_url is null; repo README has no benchmark data. Vendor measurement on Intel hardware. Hardware-gated, so not a drop-in software speedup. A verifier should open the ADMS 2025 paper for a peer-reviewed tier B check.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Intel Query Processing Library QPL IAA deflate compression throughput compared to zlib zstd'

name: LZSA
workload: Compression ratio and relative decompression speed on a ZX Spectrum/C64 file set (1,289,127 bytes) plus Canterbury, Silesia, Calgary, Large and enwik9 corpora; speed measured on 8-bit Z80/6502 decompressors.
claimed_speedup: README table, 'Decompression speed vs. LZ4': LZSA1 90% (ratio 57.08%), LZSA2 75% (52.49%), LZ4_HC -19 -B4 -BD 100% (60.59%); prose says the formats range 'from decompressing faster than LZ4 on 8-bit systems with better compression' to ZX7-like ratio. Silesia: LZSA2 32.52% versus the LZ4_HC column in the README.
tradeoffs: Targets 8-bit decompressors in assembly; the host-side packer is portable C (matchfinder.c is CC0 from wimlib) but compression is about 2x slower than LZ4_HC. Not a modern x86/Arm speed play.
caveats: Weak speed claim: the table values read as speed relative to LZ4 (90% and 75%), which is slower than LZ4, and the win is mainly compression ratio. A search snippet quotes LZSA1 as up to 9% faster to decompress on Z80, which I did not see on the README page. Benchmark scope is tiny retro-computing files; no host CPU, compiler or flags. Last commit is over 3 years old (listed as abandoned).
